title: Unique, infinite, or none
intro: For AX = B, the determinant opens the question and (adj A)·B closes it. Sort each situation by its consistency verdict.

buckets.label: Unique solution
buckets.hint: det A ≠ 0 — lines intersect at a point

buckets.label: Infinitely many
buckets.hint: det A = 0 and (adj A)·B = 0 — same line twice

buckets.label: No solution
buckets.hint: det A = 0 and (adj A)·B ≠ 0 — parallel lines

cards.text: A nodal-analysis admittance matrix with a proper ground reference and independent loops
An attitude matrix with det = +1, solving for a body-frame vector
det A = 0, and (adj A)·B comes out non-zero
A sensor-fusion system given two measurements that contradict each other after calibration drift
det A = 0, and (adj A)·B is the zero vector
A floating network: every node equation is expressible from the others, and the sources are consistent with that dependence

debrief: The pair x + y = 3 with 2x + 2y = 7, against x + y = 3 with 2x + 2y = 6, is the whole lesson in four lines. **Both have det A = 0** — identical coefficient matrices — so the determinant cannot tell them apart. What separates them is the right-hand side: doubling the first equation demands 6, so 7 is a contradiction (parallel lines, no solution) and 6 is a restatement (one line, infinitely many). That is exactly what the `(adj A)·B` test detects. Why it matters in practice: a singular system is **not** automatically unsolvable. 'Infinitely many' means your model is underdetermined — add a constraint, pick a reference node, fix a gauge, and you get an answer. 'No solution' means your inputs disagree, and no amount of extra structure fixes it; something upstream is wrong, like the drifted sensor. Those two call for opposite responses, and the determinant alone would have you treat them the same.
